normative.heap-allocation: A program shall not fail to explicitly deallocate heap-obtained storage, as omission permits memory to accumulate and exhaust available resources.
normative.stack-storage: A program shall not perform explicit deallocation of stack-allocated storage, since such storage is automatically reclaimed upon scope exit.
normative.double-release: A program shall not release the same storage block more than once, as subsequent releases corrupt the allocator metadata and produce undefined behavior.
normative.use-after-release: A program shall not access storage after it has been returned to the system, as the allocator may have reassigned that storage to a different purpose.
normative.dangling-reference: A program shall not dereference a reference to storage that no longer exists, as the referenced memory location may now be inaccessible or hold unrelated data.
normative.null-dereference: A program shall not dereference a null pointer or reference, as such dereferencing accesses unmapped memory and causes immediate failure.
normative.deallocation-form-mismatch: A program shall not use scalar deallocation to free array-allocated storage or vice versa, as the deallocation routine expects metadata and layout that match the allocation form.
normative.wrong-allocator-family: A program shall not deallocate storage through an allocator family other than the one that performed the original allocation, as each family maintains incompatible pool metadata.
normative.ownership-transfer-ambiguity: A program shall not pass a resource across an interface without establishing which side bears responsibility for release, as ambiguity produces either leaks or premature deallocation.
normative.shared-ownership: A program implementing shared ownership shall not deallocate a resource prematurely when one owner completes, as other active owners are then using invalid storage.
normative.lock-not-released: A program shall not exit any code path while still holding an exclusive lock, as doing so starves or deadlocks other threads waiting for that resource.
normative.lock-held-across-blocking-call: A program shall not retain an exclusive lock across a blocking or waiting operation that does not require the lock to be held, as unnecessary lock contention increases deadlock risk and reduces concurrency.

advisory.heap-allocation: Request memory from the system at runtime when you can't know the size in advance, but you must explicitly return it when done.
advisory.stack-storage: Declare variables on the stack inside a function, and they're automatically cleaned up the instant the function returns or the block exits.
advisory.double-release: Never free the same block twice; once it's back in the system, trying to free it again corrupts the heap.
advisory.use-after-release: Don't read or write a pointer after you've freed it; the memory is no longer yours and may have been reassigned.
advisory.dangling-reference: Keep references alive only as long as the objects they point to exist; a stale reference can't protect you from accessing destroyed memory.
advisory.null-dereference: Always check that a pointer is non-null before dereferencing; following null crashes or causes undefined behavior.
advisory.deallocation-form-mismatch: Use the matching cleanup for how you allocated: delete for new, delete[] for new[], free for malloc—mismatched forms corrupt the heap.
advisory.wrong-allocator-family: Don't mix allocator families; memory from malloc belongs with free, and memory from new belongs with delete, never the reverse.
advisory.ownership-transfer-ambiguity: Be explicit at API boundaries about who owns and must release a resource; silence breeds leaks and double-frees.
advisory.shared-ownership: When multiple independent code paths hold the same resource, use reference counting or a shared_ptr so it's released only after the last user is done.
advisory.lock-not-released: Always release a lock on every code path that acquires it, including error handlers; forgetting even one path deadlocks your program.
advisory.lock-held-across-blocking-call: Don't hold a lock during a sleep, I/O, or network call; you'll starve other threads and hold the lock far longer than necessary.

reference.heap-allocation: Storage for data is allocated dynamically at runtime for a quantity specified during program execution, and the program must explicitly deallocate it.
reference.stack-storage: Storage for data is created automatically upon entry to a scope and is automatically reclaimed when that scope is exited.
reference.double-release: The same block of allocated storage is deallocated multiple times, returning it to the system's memory manager on two or more separate occasions.
reference.use-after-release: Allocated storage is read from or written to after it has been deallocated and returned to the system.
reference.dangling-reference: A reference or pointer is dereferenced to access storage that has already been deallocated or destroyed.
reference.null-dereference: A pointer that does not designate any valid address is dereferenced, attempting to access storage through an invalid reference.
reference.deallocation-form-mismatch: Storage allocated for an array is deallocated using scalar deallocation, or storage allocated for a scalar is deallocated using array deallocation.
reference.wrong-allocator-family: Storage obtained from one allocation facility (such as malloc or new) is deallocated through a different, incompatible facility (such as free or delete).
reference.ownership-transfer-ambiguity: When a resource is transferred across a function or module boundary, it is ambiguous which party is responsible for deallocating it.
reference.shared-ownership: Multiple independent parts of a program hold references to a single resource, and the resource persists until all parts have relinquished their references.
reference.lock-not-released: A thread acquires a lock protecting a critical section but fails to release it on at least one execution path.
reference.lock-held-across-blocking-call: A thread retains a lock while performing a blocking operation, such as I/O or inter-thread synchronization, that does not require the lock to be held.
